vignette:
The assault happened twelve years ago, on a warm September night after a conference. David had been a clinical psychologist for nearly two decades then, respected in his field, comfortable in his own skin. He had stopped for a drink with a colleague he trusted. The man offered him a ride home. In the car, the air grew thick with the smell of whisky on the man’s breath. David did not remember the drive, the parking lot, or the first moments of the attack. What he carried instead was a body memory: the sensation of being pinned, the weight of a hand over his mouth, the cold vinyl of the seat against his cheek. He could not put it into words, not then, not now. Sometimes, without any image at all, the terror would rise through him like a wave, leaving him breathless and confused, his hands shaking at his desk for no reason he could name.

In the months that followed, David began to feel like a stranger to himself. He had always been a man who could sit with a patient’s pain, who trusted his own steadiness. Now he felt dead inside, hollowed out. He stopped believing he was capable of the work that had once defined him. When a patient cried, he felt nothing. When they thanked him, he felt like a fraud. He had come to see himself as an object, something used and discarded, and that feeling clung to him like a second skin. A whiff of alcohol in a grocery aisle—someone’s aftershave, a spilled drink—would send a spike of cold through his chest, and suddenly he was no longer a psychologist in a store but a thing without will, and the thought *I am nothing* would arrive before he could stop it. He began to notice discomfort everywhere: the way a colleague stood too close, the pressure of a handshake, the heat of a crowded elevator. Each small bodily discomfort felt like a warning, and each warning confirmed that he was no longer the man who could handle such things.

The more he believed he was incapable, the harder he pushed the memory away. He would feel it coming—the pressure, the smell, the helplessness—and he would slam a door on it before it could fully arrive. He could not tell his wife what had happened; the event would not become language. He could only say, *I don’t want to talk about it.* His silence became a habit, then a wall. At work, he started scheduling only morning sessions, avoiding the after-hours hallway where the air was stale and the lights hummed. He told himself it was efficiency, but he knew the truth: he was shrinking his life to fit inside a space where nothing could trigger him. But the triggers followed him. A siren on the street outside his office would make him freeze, mid-sentence, and he would feel the old numbness spread through his chest like a sedative. The numbness confirmed he was broken. The brokenness made him push the memory away again.

The cycle tightened over the years. At fifty, David was still practicing, but barely. He had stopped writing, stopped presenting, stopped taking difficult cases. He sat in his office with the blinds half-drawn, waiting for the day to end. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday in March. He had been walking to his car when a teenager stumbled out of a bar, laughing, reeking of liquor, and David had stood frozen on the sidewalk, his heart hammering, his mind blank, feeling nothing but the cold certainty that he was not a person anymore. He had gone home and told his wife he needed to find someone to talk to. He was afraid of what he might find if he opened the door to that memory. But he was more afraid of what would happen if he did not.
